Calculating camera count and coverage zones

From the customer’s task to camera count: position by coverage zone, not by wall

Start with the task, not the floor plan

The camera count follows from what the customer needs to distinguish: a face, a number plate or an event. Each task requires a different pixel density per metre and therefore a different number of cameras for the same area.

Three pixel densities
Event detection: at least 25 pixels per metre
Person recognition: at least 125
Face identification: at least 250

Choosing a server for 64+ cameras

DuoStation and NeuroStation: what to calculate beyond channel count

You opened this resource 7 September. It already counts toward resources read. Complete the unit separately for eligibility.
Channels are not the only limit

A server is limited by total recording bitrate and simultaneous viewing decodes, not simply camera count. Thirty-two cameras with four workstations put more load on it than sixty-four cameras with one.

What to include in the reserve
Server-side analytics is a separate load, not a ‘free feature’
A 30% bitrate margin: the customer will add cameras within the first year
Reserve for rebuilding the recording index after a disk failure

Calculating disk capacity for 64 cameras

Retention, bitrate and reserve: justify capacity with a calculation, not a guess

The formula and three adjustments

The basic calculation is the same as for recording retention. Three adjustments are often forgotten: index overhead, changes in bitrate during motion and free space that must remain available to prevent irregular overwriting.

How to justify the figure to the customer

Bring the calculation and its inputs, not just the total. The customer challenges the lack of transparency, not the capacity: a line reading ‘64 cameras × 4 Mbps × 30 days’ can resolve the disagreement in a minute.
